decisions.quote: In their paper of 2011 titled Gender and Philosophical Intuition Wesley Buckwalter and Stephen Stich argue that the intuitions of women and men differ significantly on various types of philosophical questions. Furthermore, men’s intuitions, so the authors, are more in line with traditionally accepted solutions of classical problems. This inherent bias, so the argument, is one of the factors that leads more men than women to pursue degrees and careers in philosophy. We attempted to replicate three of the classes of questions that Buckwalter and Stich review in their paper and for which they report significant differences. We failed to replicate the results. In specific we attempted replication of Section 3.2 and 3.8 in Buckwalter and Stich (2011).
decisions.reason: The abstract explicitly states that the author empirically re-tested the gender differences in philosophical intuitions reported in Sections 3.1, 3.2, and 3.8 of Wesley Buckwalter and Stephen Stich (2011), titled 'Gender and Philosophical Intuition', in new participant samples and failed to find significant gender differences. Although only the title and abstract are available in the primary source text, the abstract itself explicitly provides the target's authors, year (2011), exact title, and empirical comparison; no DOI is printed in the source text. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 521) is Knobe (2012) ('Experimental Philosophy', DOI 10.1093/oxfordhb/9780195309799.013.0022), a different author's handbook chapter that is not an alternate report of Buckwalter and Stich (2011). No prior adjudication file existed for this work.
